executive_assessment.text: Niger faces material and increasing climate pressure, but current food and livelihood crises cannot be reduced to climate scarcity. Supporting evidence: NER-E-001-004, E-014-021; pathways NER-P-001-003. In particular, the relatively strong 2025 aggregate cereal harvest alongside localized weather and insecurity impacts demonstrates why national averages and deterministic scarcity narratives are inadequate. (FAOHome)

The best-supported Climate-FCV mechanisms operate through livelihoods, mobility, land/water access, displacement, institutions and service delivery - not a direct climate -> violence relationship. Supporting evidence: NER-E-016-019, E-022-023, E-028-030; pathways NER-P-001-006 and P-008. (SIPRI)

Niger has substantial adaptation policy architecture and some evaluated resilience gains, but implementation, financing, local capacity, data and current independent evaluation remain material constraints. Supporting evidence: NER-E-005-009, E-012-013, E-024-027; pathways NER-P-005-008.

geographic_notes.text: National aggregates obscure substantial variation. Tillabéri and Diffa combine insecurity, displacement and agricultural-access problems; Tahoua also hosts substantial displaced populations and appears in older pastoral-resource evidence. Diffa stands out in the current IPC nutrition analysis, while Agadez appears in refugee-site nutrition evidence and has distinct pastoral/desert livelihood characteristics. (FAOHome)

The 2014 findings on farmer-herder conflict, Rural Code implementation and Louma's land commission are local historical evidence and must not be represented as the current condition of all Tillabéri, Tahoua or Niger. (ResearchGate)

Lake Chad climate-security findings are relevant primarily to the eastern basin/Diffa context. SIPRI explicitly studies a transboundary region spanning Niger, Nigeria, Chad and Cameroon; its recruitment and resource-tension pathways are not national Niger estimates. (SIPRI)

Tillabéri, Diffa and Dosso feature in UNICEF's 2026 evidence of conflict-related humanitarian/service constraints, while IPC identifies different patterns for malnutrition, including Diffa, selected Maradi departments and refugee sites. These different geographies should not be collapsed into a single “climate-FCV hotspot” category.

Important underrepresented settings include Niamey and secondary-city heat exposure, groundwater-dependent systems, Agadez desert/oasis livelihoods, Niger River floodplain communities beyond the available humanitarian reporting, and contemporary transhumance corridors outside the older field sites.

sector_notes.text: Coverage is strongest for agriculture, livestock/pastoralism, food security, humanitarian delivery, health/nutrition, water/WASH, land governance and DRM. Climate information and social protection/anticipatory action are reasonably represented at policy or programme-output level.

Coverage is thinner for groundwater quantity and governance, fisheries, urban heat/productivity, transport disruption, energy-system climate resilience, ecosystem services, private-sector adaptation and the distributional effects of adaptation finance. The NAP includes forestry, transport and wetlands as priorities, but this packet found less evaluated sector performance in those areas. (UNDP)

known_gaps.text: Climate projections: the principal nationally specific projection evidence verified here uses CMIP5/RCP4.5-8.5. A current, downscaled CMIP6 assessment for Niger's livelihood zones, river basins and cities is needed before using precise future hazard estimates.

Causal Climate-FCV evidence: current Niger-specific longitudinal or quasi-experimental evidence remains scarce. The strongest Niger-specific field evidence located is from 2014; broader SIPRI evidence explicitly characterizes the West African literature as limited. (SIPRI)

Post-2023 institutional change: how Niger's changed political, fiscal, decentralization and international-financing environment affects NAP/NDC implementation at commune and regional levels has not been independently evaluated in the sources reviewed.

FCV-to-climate direction: current sources demonstrate insecurity disrupting farms, markets, mobility and services, but rarely measure how much this reduces actual adaptation outcomes or increases climate-attributable loss.

Differentiated vulnerability: children, refugees, IDPs, women and pastoral groups appear in the evidence, but comparable quantitative analysis by sex, age, livelihood, disability, displacement status and wealth across hazards is missing.

Mobility: evidence does not support treating migration or pastoral mobility as automatically climate-caused. Current data capable of separating climate, security, economic, family and border-policy motives were not verified in an accessible national dataset.
Farmer-herder relations: the most detailed Niger evidence is old. Current conditions following escalating insecurity and political change may differ substantially.
Response effectiveness: current UNICEF, UNHCR, FAO and national documents provide outputs, plans and operational reporting but generally do not establish counterfactual programme effectiveness.

Unintended effects: apart from IFAD's documented budget trade-off and older land-access/maladaptation findings, systematic evidence on adaptation creating exclusion, conflict, elite capture, groundwater depletion or livelihood displacement is thin.

Access/verification: the UNHCR PDF binary could not be rendered; claims were restricted to its accessible publication page. Screenshot rendering also intermittently failed for several otherwise text-accessible PDFs.

*None are entirely absent, but coping-capacity, response-performance, direct-climate-fcv and resilience-peace-capacity are only partially covered. Direct Climate-FCV and peace-capacity evidence is especially constrained by age, locality or regional scope.
